scale.score: 0-5 capability strength/readiness for James's reliable multi-agent operations. 0 no implementation after scoped inspection; 1 narrow prototype; 2 partial/major limits; 3 useful implemented; 4 mature design with substantial coverage; 5 comprehensive and proven operationally (never given from docs/source alone). null means unknown or not applicable.
scale.criticality: 1-5 importance for James's reliable multi-agent operations, not market importance.
scale.evidence_tier: The tier the score chiefly rests on. supporting_tiers lists any extra narrow evidence (live = observed in this audit session itself).
scale.aggregation: No totals. Rows overlap (C01/C18/C25; C14/C15). Ours = the best combined contribution of BORG, Memory, Plimsoll and ecosystem components; component_detail separates them.

ours.finding: Deep Codex app-server bridge: pinned runtime, role instructions, identity-checked resume, fail-closed replies to approval requests. The Grok bridge resumes CLI sessions, but the installer does not provision it and the docs say to leave it disabled. BORG core's Claude path is a detached 'claude -p' that ignores packet.model and never tracks exit. The stack drives subscription CLI agents, which Omnara cannot. Claude-seat delegation in the ecosystem is live in this very run (fleet-delegate worker on Studio1). There is no API-protocol abstraction and no cross-provider failover.

BORG.note: Codex deep; Grok gated and unprovisioned; Claude launch-only

Memory.note: local Ollama models are used only for extraction (see C12)

Plimsoll.note: observes four runtimes; does not route

Ecosystem.note: fleet-delegate Claude seats (live: this run); Cursor/Grok fleet control documented in the tools directory, not verified

omnara.finding: Three wire protocols (OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages) with OpenRouter and Bedrock variants and custom endpoints. Grants and model revisions are resolved on every call. Provider replay identity lets a conversation switch providers safely. Retries are classified, honour Retry-After and stop after 8. Gaps: no cross-provider failover. It runs its own harness on API keys and cannot drive subscription CLI agents (C25). Its production network filter blocks private, loopback and 100.64.0.0/10 (Tailscale) model endpoints. The docs say revoking a grant spares running agents; the code enforces the grant on every call.

rows.name: durable agent state and crash recovery

ours.finding: Evidence durability is strong. The router records intent and receipt before admission, with create-only writes. A lost response becomes UNKNOWN_DO_NOT_RETRY. After a crash, connector receipts become outcome_unknown. The vendored Inbox uses SQLite WAL with leases and a crash-safe client outbox. Execution recovery is weak: the conductor keeps its thread map and events in process memory, and recovery is manual. Verified cliff: no shipped code writes COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED or RECONCILED_NO_START (only PRE_START_FAILED). The ledger scan rejects above 10,000 entries or 4 MiB, and a failed scan refuses all dispatch. dispatch.lock has no stale-PID recovery.

BORG.note: durable fail-closed receipts; in-memory conductor; self-locking router ledger

Plimsoll.note: durable spool and outbox cover telemetry only

Ecosystem.note: vendored Inbox: WAL, leases, same-transaction receipts, client outbox; estate account recovery documented, not verified

omnara.finding: Postgres-authoritative kernel. A trigger makes agent_events immutable, with a unique sequence and idempotency key per agent. Each agent has one lease-fenced runtime lock (90 s default) renewed at about a third of the lease. Maintenance reaps expired locks every second, marks in-flight model calls outcome_ambiguous and running tools 'external outcome unknown'. The daemon keeps process reports in a SQLite outbox. Limits: a single Postgres point of failure with no HA or backup guidance; SIGTERM cancels in-flight turns with no drain, so deploys re-run model calls; model calls are at-least-once.

ours.finding: Codex: native turn/steer guarded by expectedTurnId, plus turn/interrupt and thread/resume. Grok: steering is interrupt then resume. Claude: no steering. Events are polled from one 5,000-event in-memory ring shared by all threads, with no gap signal and no push stream. Steering is reachable only through unauthenticated loopback HTTP, not through MCP or any UI.

BORG.note: real mid-turn Codex steering; lossy polled events

Ecosystem.note: Inbox instructions give asynchronous redirection at agent checkpoints, not turn steering

omnara.finding: Inputs are queued, steering or immediate, under a DB-enforced state machine. The backlog supports list, move, promote, demote and cancel. Cancel goes through the database and Redis, falls back to lease renewal, and uses an idempotent cancel_current key. Config can change mid-run. Steering waits for in-flight tool batches (it does not preempt); there is no pause/resume or unarchive; open approvals never expire.

ours.finding: The Inbox has the most sophisticated authority model in either stack: leased deliveries; authority re-validated at delivery time, so lapsed instructions are rejected before lease; compare-and-set reassignment; delegable grants whose expiry cannot exceed the parent's. Beads is pinned upstream. But BORG's router and launch bus never consult the Inbox or Beads, the Inbox runtime hook ships unwired, and nothing links a dispatch receipt to an assignment or issue. Poison messages redeliver with no cap, and each BORG install has its own hub. Live: this audit was delegated from Studio0 to a Claude seat on Studio1, and the Inbox hook registered this session.

BORG.note: role dispatch and launch bus only; no lineage; ignores the Inbox and Beads

Plimsoll.note: lane-receipt ownership census is library code called only by proof scripts

Ecosystem.note: Inbox engine is strong (about 4 as a component) but weakly integrated; fleet-delegate live in this run; shared estate hub documented only

omnara.finding: Built-in spawn/read/send/stop/list subagent tools. Spawn is transactional and idempotent, keyed by tool call ID, with per-key instance, total and depth caps (depth defaults to 1, maximum 8). Child results return to the parent as steering input, and children share the parent's machines. Tree only: no peer messaging, shared task ledger, work claims or ownership model. Children start with only the task string.

ours.finding: SSH fleet routing is identity-pinned. Enrollment verifies the target's identity. Every fleet_call re-pins identity, checks the target's tool schema and reports not_started or outcome_unknown. SSH runs with BatchMode, StrictHostKeyChecking=yes and '--'. It routes tools only: no memory, Inbox or conductor lanes are replicated. Conductor lanes must bind 127.0.0.1, and no remote capacity collectors ship. remote_tools hard-codes macOS sysctl and /bin/zsh. Whoever holds the controller's SSH keys has owner authority on every target.

BORG.note: identity-pinned SSH MCP tool routing; macOS-specific remote jobs

Memory.note: fleet peer hook gives remote machines scoped recall and capture over tunnels

Plimsoll.note: one collector per machine; fleet-operations rollout is library-only

Ecosystem.note: seven-Mac estate documented; fleet-delegate shipped this packet to Studio1 (live)

omnara.finding: One outbound-only daemon (HTTPS/WSS) serves both your own machines and sandboxes. A local SQLite outbox and runner custody survive restarts. After a 30 s grace, waiting calls get machine_unreachable without the process being killed. Every tool takes a machine_id, and machines can be added or removed at runtime. Risks: run_command defaults to always_allow; your own machines get no OS isolation; daemon tokens have no expiry column; self-update verifies only a SHA-256 from the same origin.

ours.finding: No cloud sandbox lifecycle found. The search covered docker, podman, container, firecracker, e2b, modal, daytona, devcontainer, kubernetes, ec2 and fly.io over the connector, coordination, installer, docs, platform and conductor. The vendored Tart supervisor gives disposable, digest-pinned local macOS VM desktop leases with verified cleanup, but it is off by default, desktop-only and not wired by the installer. BORG's conductor defaults Codex to danger-full-access.

BORG.note: only passes Codex local sandbox modes through; default is full access

Ecosystem.note: vendored Tart desktop lease; estate Tart enrollment proof documented only

omnara.finding: Blaxel, Daytona, Modal and Unikraft sit behind one idempotent provisioning contract: record before the external call, with deterministic allocation names. Provider runtimes are reconciled and idle machines deleted, with count caps at pool, project, agent and org level, plus sleep/wake. No warm pools and no dollar caps. Orphan runtime protection is opt-in. Modal has a hard 24-hour limit.

ours.finding: BORG ships a thin CDP browser (selector click and insertText, a fresh profile per session) and coordinate-only AppleScript UI behind a single desktop lock. The public release refuses the richer Peekaboo backend at config load, and the fleet_browser Playwright worker script is not shipped. The ecosystem browser/desktop broker is documented as a restricted pilot; its current state is unverified.

BORG.note: minimal CDP and AppleScript tools

Ecosystem.note: documented restricted pilot with quarantines (tools directory entry 'Fleet browser and isolated desktop broker'); not verified

omnara.finding: Only static web_fetch (no JavaScript) and Exa web_search. No browser automation or desktop control found; the search covered playwright, puppeteer, computer-use, chromedp, xdotool, screenshot and vnc. Without an Exa key, search queries go to Exa's public keyless MCP endpoint by default.

ours.finding: An authenticated FastMCP gateway with about 60 tools (files, processes, jobs, browser, UI, credentials, fleet) and a versioned, schema-fingerprinted manifest. A stdio proxy keeps the bearer out of client config. A Cloudflare Access gateway serves web ChatGPT, and fleet_call reaches other hosts. The memory MCP adds 11 scoped tools. Gaps: owners cannot mount custom tools or MCP servers; skills are just paths; tool search is a substring match; the manifest names tools that do not exist. Most extensibility in practice comes from the native Codex and Claude MCP/skills support.

BORG.note: strong native tool gateway; no owner extensions

Ecosystem.note: many estate MCP servers documented; not verified

omnara.finding: Remote MCP (stateless and session protocols) with bearer, OAuth or SigV4 auth and a leased OAuth refresh. Also deferred tools with tool_search, durable custom tools (first result wins), versioned and granted skills synced to machines, and Omnara's own API as about 75 MCP tools. Gaps: no stdio MCP. The worker blocks private, loopback and 100.64.0.0/10 MCP hosts, so tailnet or LAN servers need public HTTPS. MCP timeouts are fixed at 30 s and 5 minutes.

ours.finding: One local Qdrant store, 11 MCP tools and default-closed recall hooks for Codex, Claude, Grok and remote hosts, with per-principal hashed tokens and scope filters. The boundary is thin. stdio gets full access by design. Hooks and tools reach Qdrant directly, and the installer binds Qdrant to loopback without an API key. memory_search tells agents to use memory FIRST, with no candidate framing. No repo tests cover MCP scope enforcement. Single node.

BORG.note: packages the memory; installer defaults every principal to '*' scopes

Memory.note: recall shared across four runtimes; thin boundary

Ecosystem.note: shared Mem0 service documented in the tools directory; deliberately not queried, to keep the audit independent

omnara.finding: No shared or cross-agent memory, vector store or retrieval tool found. The search covered embedding, pgvector, vector, rag, knowledge base, semantic search, memory and recall over internal, cmd, migrations, docs and api. The only hit was an embedding-model filter. What exists is per-agent context compaction and human-uploaded skills.

ours.finding: Graphiti on FalkorDB, partitioned per scope with collision-checked keys and bitemporal edges. Every row is stamped derived_unverified. At recall time a graph fact is shown only while its bound source rows still exist unchanged, live and unretired. Limits: it is opt-in; local extraction is slow (420 s per episode); no FalkorDB backup was found; the installed adapter reads through the write-capable graph.query, while the public copy uses ro_query.

BORG.note: packages the graph layer

omnara.finding: No graph store or recall tool found. There is a strong provenance substrate a recall layer could build on: an immutable, sequenced event log, and checkpoints that record the producing model call and the event frontier.

ours.finding: The newest Codex/fleet capture path requires user or tool evidence references and checks that literals appear in that evidence. Retention is marker-based, journaled, capped and reversible; decay and vacuum never hard-delete without confirmation. But the paper's merge/contradiction consolidation is held in the public copy and off by default in the installed runtime, and the dream tests skip at import. MCP memory_delete is an immediate hard delete with no receipt, and deleted text persists in retired-log with no erasure path. The Plimsoll collector keeps raw rows 90 days and has purge commands.

Memory.note: grounded capture, reversible retention; no erasure; untested dream

Plimsoll.note: collector retention and purge; the Cloud has no telemetry retention

omnara.finding: Per-agent compaction is well tested (checkpoints, bounded progressive summaries). There is no cross-session capture and no forgetting. Triggers reject UPDATE and DELETE on events, content blocks, model outputs and tool results. Org and project deletion is a soft delete, while the docs say it 'removes everything'.

ours.finding: Extraction and embeddings run fully locally on pinned Ollama models, with a grammar shim, opt-in LoRA training chains with crash resume, and an exam plus a promotion canary for each Graphiti call shape. The canary caught a 400/400 exam winner failing in the real pipeline. All three published adapters are benched and uncanaried. There is no automated promotion, the harness is MLX/Apple Silicon only, the scoring logic is untested, and none of it runs in CI.

BORG.note: the training and eval harness ships in the BORG repo

omnara.finding: Custom OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoints are allowed. But base URLs must be HTTPS unless loopback, and the model network filter rejects private addresses in all modes and loopback outside insecure dev mode. A production self-host therefore cannot reach a LAN, tailnet or same-host Ollama, although the README names Ollama. No eval or training tooling found.

rows.name: human operator dashboard and streaming interaction

ours.finding: BORG ships only the vendored Inbox web console (coordination actions, 30 s polling) and conductor JSON endpoints. There is no agent-session view, steering UI or push stream. Plimsoll's local and Cloud dashboards are spend and outcome analytics with no agent interaction, and the Cloud manager view samples 1,000 events. The ecosystem's Estate Ops and Grafana are documented as read-only fleet views; not verified here.

BORG.note: conductor JSON endpoints only

Ecosystem.note: Inbox console (source); Estate Ops and Grafana documented only

omnara.finding: Resumable SSE (sequence IDs, Last-Event-ID, 10 s heartbeat) and an auto-reconnecting SDK shared by the CLI and the React package. The web dashboard covers agents, the input queue, interactions, usage and resources, and there is a bidirectional Slack connector. Gaps: tool-call updates and deltas are not replayed; approvals are per agent only; Slack approvals bypass Omnara roles.

rows.name: team identity, project boundaries and RBAC

ours.finding: [Sharing note: private Cloud hardening details retained in the private original; rating unchanged.]

BORG.note: single owner_all principal

Memory.note: scope ACL; read implies write and delete; no expiry

Ecosystem.note: Inbox delegable grants; no delegation tests found

omnara.finding: Every OpenAPI operation must map to an authorization policy or the server refuses to start. Org and project roles are derived in SQL. Tokens are typed and hashed, passwords use Argon2id, OIDC/GitHub login is supported, and secrets, machines, pools, models and skills are shared by grant. Personal tokens and org keys have no scopes or expiry; there are no custom roles, SAML, SCIM or admin audit log.

rows.name: human approvals, tool permissions and secrets isolation

ours.finding: Secrets handling is strong: tool arguments and results are scanned for secret shapes (including the install's own tokens), credential handles are value-blind, and private files must be 0600, single-link and symlink-free. Permission scoping is absent. The conductor starts Codex with danger-full-access and approvalPolicy never, and Grok runs --always-approve. The connector is one owner_all principal, and the Cloudflare gateway gives web ChatGPT that full tool set, reaching every enrolled host through fleet_call. The conductor HTTP API has no authentication and exposes a raw /rpc passthrough on loopback. James's doctrine rejects approval gates; the gap that matters is who can reach the control plane.

BORG.note: good secret isolation; no scoping; unauthenticated conductor

Memory.note: stdio full access; loopback databases without auth

Plimsoll.note: per-source producer tokens and a management credential locally

Ecosystem.note: vault and value-blind secrets hub documented only

omnara.finding: Per-tool allow/ask/deny, with approvals bound to the exact canonical input and a DB-enforced interaction state machine. Secrets use AES-256-GCM envelope encryption; egress passes a network filter; logs are scrubbed. Defaults are permissive: built-in tools including run_command are always_allow. Resolving an approval needs the same permission as sending input. Slack approvals check only the Slack signature and target, with no Omnara role. Secrets injected as environment variables are readable by run_command and persist in immutable tool output. Only a local key wrapper exists, and insecure dev mode uses a fixed, public encryption key.

ours.finding: Hooks are central to our stack. Codex lifecycle hooks are installed through Codex's config API with compare-and-set and readback. Memory has recall and capture hooks for Codex, Claude and Grok, and Plimsoll wires hooks and OTLP for telemetry. Services run under launchd/systemd with a budgeted watchdog. Live in this session: the Inbox and Jev hooks injected identity, checkpoint health and the policy hash at session start and on tool use. Gaps: no scheduler in BORG source, notifications are local files, and there is no push or email.

BORG.note: verified Codex hooks and watchdog; no scheduler

Plimsoll.note: managed hooks with a durable spool

Ecosystem.note: Inbox and Jev hooks observed live in this session; automations documented

omnara.finding: Idempotent cron triggers (keyed by trigger ID and due time) and Standard-Webhooks event webhooks from a DB outbox, with optional signing and a 10-minute delivery window, plus bidirectional Slack. Gaps: cron is undocumented, webhooks drop after 10 minutes, email covers auth only, and there are no push notifications.

rows.name: capacity-aware fleet admission and work ownership

ours.finding: The design is ahead of Omnara's. Router admission fails closed on unknown, stale, unreachable, hot or memory-saturated capacity and on unknown claims. Workspace conflicts are judged by realpath plus device/inode ancestry. The connector has resource-scoped locks with 64-in-flight/256-queued admission. Live: this host's seat gate admitted this run's subagents on measured load per core, memory, pressure, open files and disk. But the shipped router never writes terminal receipt states, so a dispatched workspace stays claimed until the JSON is hand-edited. No remote capacity collectors ship, and remote_tools uses a fixed 1.5 load/core test with no memory check.

BORG.note: excellent collision logic; missing reconciliation

Ecosystem.note: seat gate probed live on Studio1; Inbox fleet context and Estate Ops documented only

omnara.finding: Work ownership is excellent: one leased lock per agent, SKIP LOCKED claims, and a pool machine attached to one agent at a time. Admission is static: 4 turns per worker by default, declared pool CPU/memory quotas and object-count limits. There is no measured host load, no admission for your own machines, and no tenant fairness (global FIFO). The per-org managed-work kill switch has no writer in the repository.

ours.finding: The router pins each Codex lane to an account digest and reads native rate-limit windows with freshness checks. It ranks lanes by remaining allowance, breaking ties by reset time, and separates exhaustion from spend-control. It falls back only before native start and never retries an uncertain start on another account. Limits: it acts at admission time only, covers Codex only, and ships an empty model-to-bucket map. Plimsoll's allowance adapters are unwired, and its doctrine forbids using them for routing. Ecosystem manager recovery and retarget is documented with receipts but not verified here.

BORG.note: Codex allowance ranking at admission

Plimsoll.note: unwired observation adapters; default profiles only

Ecosystem.note: documented account recovery and retarget with exhaustion-triggered successors; not verified in this audit

omnara.finding: Retries the same provider up to 8 times, honouring Retry-After, and passes an OpenRouter model list through. Billing and quota errors are terminal. Hosted credits are enforced by an external kill switch. No allowance tracking, account pools, reset awareness or use of subscription seats.

ours.finding: Plimsoll captures Claude Code and Codex hooks, OTLP and history rollouts across every configured seat and profile. It records cost provenance (reported, estimated or unknown), deduplicates live capture against file tailers, and never shows unpriced usage as $0. Limits: the 15-model price table is hand-maintained with a prefix fallback and has no Gemini, Grok or gpt-5.6+ prices. Grok token capture is unproven, the bill-reconciliation gate is red, and it is macOS only. BORG records allowance percentage only.

BORG.note: allowance percentage in receipts only

Memory.note: queue and health metrics; no token accounting

Plimsoll.note: mature for Claude and Codex; thin elsewhere

omnara.finding: Per-call token breakdown with DB invariants and exact provider-reported cost; a usage API at org, project, profile and agent scope; the UI flags calls that reported no cost. Only its own agents are covered, and there are no budgets, alerts, price-based estimates or token metrics.

rows.name: shipped outcome linkage and value measurement

ours.finding: Plimsoll joins sessions to pull requests through linkage keys and allocates tokens with conservation checks. It computes Validated Delivery Yield, keeps an immutable outcome timeline and marks unproven results UNKNOWN. The Cloud records human acceptance attestations. But the project's own audit found only 13 of 2,423 sessions linked and judged fleet cost per merged PR not publishable. Linkage is GitHub-only and run by hand per repo. BORG routes report completionVerified:false, and the Inbox reports work_acceptance:not_asserted. [Editorial date: this linkage figure comes from 20 August 2026; current coverage was not verified.]

BORG.note: honest non-claims and opaque outcome references only

Plimsoll.note: careful design; low measured live coverage

Ecosystem.note: Beads acceptance is upstream; not assessed

omnara.finding: No linkage of runs to commits, pull requests, deploys or business outcomes, and no value metric. Only tool-call outcomes and agent activity states exist. The search covered pull request, commit, outcome, kpi, roi, deliverable and acceptance over internal and migrations.

rows.name: privacy suppression and selective data collection

ours.finding: Plimsoll's collector suppresses raw content before anything is stored, with allowlist-first admission, and locks managed installs to metadata-only. Its privacy spec is generated from code. But protected identifiers are unsalted SHA-256 truncated to 16 hex characters, so a dictionary reverses them, and a project issue records doing exactly that. Memory is weaker. The older Claude/Grok capture hook stores first, deletes matches afterwards and logs the dropped text. The public identifier floor fails open when its config is missing; the installed runtime fails closed. There is no at-rest encryption and no erasure.

BORG.note: secret redaction in tool I/O; training capture opt-in

Memory.note: best path redacts before extraction; older paths store then delete

Plimsoll.note: strong collector suppression; reversible hashes; Cloud deletion only partial

omnara.finding: Logs are scrubbed, OpenAI requests use store:false, and no product telemetry was found. But all inputs, outputs, reasoning and tool results are stored as plaintext content blocks that cannot be updated or deleted. End-user actors cannot be deleted. Without an Exa key, web_search sends queries to Exa's keyless public endpoint.

rows.name: idempotency, audit receipts and acceptance evidence

ours.finding:
Broad but uneven. What works:
- Inbox request_id receipts commit in the same transaction, with parameter-hash conflict detection.
- Router intents are duplicate-safe.
- Memory verified findings use deterministic IDs, locks, read-back and RETRYABLE_UNKNOWN.
- The Plimsoll outbox has verified per-item acknowledgements, dead letters and replay.
- Non-claims are honest (completionVerified false).
Gaps:
- Connector receipts are not idempotency keys, so a retry can execute twice.
- The launch bus has no dedup.
- Router receipts never reach a terminal state.
- memory_add has no key, and the public release replays adds on any exception.
- memory_delete is unaudited.
- Plimsoll receipts are digests, not signatures.
- The Cloud acceptance journal has a session-setting escape hatch.

BORG.note: duplicate-safe intents; non-idempotent connector receipts

Memory.note: strong on newer paths; general add and delete weak

Plimsoll.note: idempotent delivery; unsigned receipts; contract drift

omnara.finding: DB-enforced idempotency on execution paths (events, inputs, agents, artifacts), comparing intent on replay. Deterministic system keys for cancel, spawn and cron. An immutable ledger, sha256 artifact digests and recorded ambiguous outcomes. Gaps: no admin audit log; Idempotency-Key is accepted on only 11 of 86 mutating public operations (counted by this auditor); no concept of acceptance evidence.

ours.finding: The auditor found partial identity/privacy boundaries and material hardening work in the private Cloud snapshot, plus limitations in the public components cited below. The exact private implementation details are withheld from this shareable copy; the original finding and unchanged rating are in the private archive.

BORG.note: careful single-platform installer; no upgrade path

Memory.note: public copy portable; installed copy hard-codes estate paths

omnara.finding: Digest-pinned, distroless, multi-arch images with SLSA provenance, an SBOM and cosign signing. Production config fails closed. Forward-only migrations have CI compatibility checks, and the daemon runs on macOS and Linux. But the compose defaults enable insecure dev mode: a fixed public encryption key, open signup, fixed database credentials, and Redis and Postgres published on all interfaces. The documented public-exposure recipe keeps those defaults. There is no backup, restore or down-migration guidance, and the self-hosting pages are missing from the docs navigation.

rows.name: public API/SDK, documentation and contribution readiness

ours.finding: Candid, extensive docs and papers; MIT and Apache licences; a versioned MCP manifest; 116 Plimsoll proof scripts. But there is no SDK or API spec for the conductor or Inbox HTTP APIs, and BORG has no CONTRIBUTING or SECURITY file. BORG CI runs 22 of about 301 Python tests (installer guards only) plus the conductor Node tests; memory, graph and training tests never run in CI. Plimsoll's docs have drifted: check counts disagree and the changelog stops at 0.7.5.

BORG.note: good docs; no SDK or spec; thin CI

Plimsoll.note: extensive but drifting docs; no SDK

omnara.finding: An OpenAPI spec with 149 operations kept in sync by CI; a generated TypeScript SDK, CLI and React package; and the API as MCP. There are 576 Go test files with 3,620 test functions (counted, not executed). CI covers race, integration, e2e, Playwright and live provider tests (documented in the workflows). SECURITY and CONTRIBUTING are present. It is pre-stable (security fixes land on main only) and has small doc gaps.

rows.name: subscription-seat CLI agents as execution engines (added row; overlaps C01 and C18, not aggregated)

ours.finding: The stack is built around vendor CLI agents as engines: Codex app-server lanes, one per account profile; Claude Code seats (this run is one); and Grok CLI sessions. That keeps vendor-native tools, sub-agents and subscription allowances. Depth is uneven: Codex is deep, BORG core's Claude path is launch-only, and Grok is gated.

BORG.note: Codex lanes deep; Claude and Grok thin

Ecosystem.note: fleet-delegate Claude seats live in this run; seat and account inventory documented only

omnara.finding: Omnara runs its own harness against model APIs. No adapter to drive Codex app-server, Claude Code or the Grok CLI as agent engines was found; the search for chatgpt, codex, claude code and subscription over internal, cmd and docs found only model-name pricing and MCP client docs. Those CLIs can drive Omnara through its MCP server, and an Omnara agent could shell out to a CLI via run_command, but neither is an engine integration.

rows.name: release integrity and cross-component contract consistency (added row)

ours.finding: Installed and public memory copies diverge in both directions; privacy and replay fixes differ, as do identity schema strings. The reviewer also found collector/Cloud contract drift. BORG’s release guard and hashed inventory are a strong counter-example. Private Cloud details are retained in the private original.

BORG.note: release guard and deterministic hashed inventory

Memory.note: installed and published copies diverge both ways

Plimsoll.note: copied modules drift; the capacity protocol has a fingerprint, ingest does not

omnara.finding: A single repository generates its SDK from one OpenAPI source. CI enforces API compatibility and protects released migrations, and release artifacts are signed. No installed-versus-published split was observed within the inspected scope. Omnara Cloud's private services were not assessed.

axes.name: managed execution
axes.reason: Omnara owns a durable, lease-fenced Postgres kernel with steering, subagents, machines and sandboxes. Our execution depends on vendor CLIs plus a thin conductor with in-memory state, manual recovery, lossy polled events and a self-locking router ledger. Rows: C01-C08, C25.

axes.name: collective memory
axes.reason: Ours is real, shared across four runtimes and provenance-aware, but thinly bounded, single-node and untested in CI. Omnara has only per-agent compaction and human-uploaded skills. Rows: C09-C12.

axes.name: fleet operations
axes.reason: Ours has the better admission and allowance design (fail-closed on unknown telemetry, allowance-ranked lanes; seat gate observed live), with operational cliffs. Omnara has production-grade machine custody and sandbox lifecycle, but static admission and no account routing. Rows: C05, C06, C16-C18.

axes.name: delivery economics
axes.reason: Plimsoll measures CLI-seat cost with provenance and has outcome linkage by design, though linkage coverage was last measured at 13 of 2,423 sessions. Omnara has exact provider cost for its own agents, with no value linkage and no budgets. Rows: C18-C20. [Editorial date: this linkage figure comes from 20 August 2026; current coverage was not verified.]

axes.name: product readiness
axes.reason: Omnara: contract-first API and RBAC, SDK/CLI, heavy CI and signed releases; pre-1.0 with unsafe compose defaults. Ours: macOS-only, no SDK or spec, thin CI, estate leakage and drift, and a prototype Cloud trust boundary. Rows: C13-C15, C21-C24, C26.

recommendations.title: Internal: make the BORG router self-healing. Write terminal receipt states from native thread readback, reconcile and archive receipts, recover a stale dispatch.lock by PID liveness, and alarm on ledger size.
recommendations.risk: Marking an in-flight run terminal would release its workspace claim early. Reconcile only from native readback and keep UNKNOWN when readback fails.

recommendations.title: Internal: authenticate the conductor HTTP API with a per-lane token file and Host/Origin checks; gate or remove raw /rpc; make danger-full-access and approvalPolicy never an explicit request, not the default.
recommendations.risk: Breaks existing unauthenticated callers. Coordinate with the fleet conductor owners and roll out token distribution first. Full access stays available by explicit opt-in, per James's doctrine.

recommendations.title: Adopt Omnara's durable run-ledger pattern for conductor threads: durable monotonic event sequences with replay, lease-fenced ownership, a reaper that marks in-flight work ambiguous, and no event loss on restart.
recommendations.risk: Could duplicate Codex's own rollout persistence. Keep native Codex state authoritative and store only ownership, cursors and outcomes. Apache-2.0 code needs NOTICE handling if copied; patterns do not.

recommendations.title: Carry one work correlation ID, Omnara-style (one identity per run), across router receipts, Inbox assignments, Beads issues, memory capture identity and Plimsoll sessions, so outcome linkage stops depending on git heuristics.
recommendations.risk: Schema changes across four components with separate owners. The ID must not carry private content into telemetry.

recommendations.title: Internal: close the memory boundary. Authenticate stdio or restrict it to owner processes; add Qdrant and FalkorDB auth; route MCP delete through tombstones with receipts; remove store-then-delete logging; frame memory_search results as candidates; run memory and graph tests in CI.
recommendations.risk: Hooks and tools that talk to Qdrant directly will break until they are credentialed. Stage the rollout.

recommendations.title: Internal: reconcile the installed and published memory runtimes into one source (port the privacy and replay fixes out, and the read-only graph queries in; unify the identity schema). Make the Plimsoll collector and Cloud share one package with contract fingerprints.
recommendations.risk: An identity-schema change alters deterministic memory IDs, so migrate or dual-read.

recommendations.title: Internal: Plimsoll trust and privacy. Use a per-tenant HMAC for protected identifiers; issue per-device upload secrets with rotation and revocation; require signatures by default; add database-level tenant isolation and real per-person erasure before any external customer.
recommendations.risk: Changing the hash breaks existing joins. Version the linkage keys.

recommendations.title: Adopt Omnara's fail-closed operation-to-policy table for BORG HTTP and MCP surfaces, and add scoped connector profiles (read-only, memory-only) for web and remote clients instead of owner_all only.
recommendations.risk: Owner workflows rely on full access, so keep owner_all as an explicit profile.

recommendations.title: Do not replace BORG conductors or fleet dispatch with Omnara as the fleet execution plane.
recommendations.risk: We would forgo Omnara's durability; recommendations 3, 8 and 10 import its patterns instead.

recommendations.title: Adopt idempotent spawn keys (spawn:<toolCallID>), depth and instance caps, and the queued/steering/immediate input model in fleet-delegate, the launch bus and Inbox instructions.
recommendations.risk: Small semantic changes to existing delegation flows need documentation.

recommendations.title: Internal: run the existing connector, coordination, memory, graph and training tests in CI.
recommendations.risk: Some tests may need fixtures, or may fail on first run; that is the point.

recommendations.title: Upstream to Omnara a configurable private-egress allowlist (tailnet and LAN CIDRs, default closed) plus local/stdio MCP support, unblocking self-hosted local models and private MCP such as BORG memory.
recommendations.risk: Upstream may reject it on SSRF grounds; it must stay default-closed. Any upstream send needs an orchestration-tier agent with full context.

recommendations.title: Optional bounded pilot: self-host Omnara only for API-billed, client-facing agents that need RBAC, Slack and disposable sandboxes, after hardening (dev mode off, run_command always_ask, Slack approvers restricted, memory through a scoped public-HTTPS MCP profile).
recommendations.risk: The network filter blocks tailnet services. Content is retained immutably, which conflicts with client deletion duties. It uses API billing, not seats. Without a patch, Slack users can approve with no roles. It adds a second execution plane invisible to seat admission.

recommendations.title: Report Omnara defects. Use its private security channel for the Slack approval path without role checks and for the insecure public-exposure recipe with its fixed dev key. File public issues for the doc mismatches (org deletion, grant revocation), the keyless Exa default, the missing SIGTERM drain, non-expiring daemon tokens and unverified update attestation.
recommendations.risk: Needs responsible-disclosure handling. External sends require an orchestration-tier agent after full context, so none was sent in this audit.

recommendations.title: Offer a provenance-aware memory provider (candidate framing, derived_unverified, source-currency checks) and Plimsoll-style outcome linkage as Omnara integrations over remote MCP and webhooks.
recommendations.risk: Maintenance burden and cross-tenant memory privacy; the direct value to James's operations is small.

recommendations.title: Add an Omnara source adapter to Plimsoll (usage API plus event webhooks) if any Omnara pilot runs, so its agents join the same cost and outcome ledger.
recommendations.risk: Omnara webhooks drop after 10 minutes, so reconcile from the usage API.

limitations: Source and documentation only. No product tests, builds or services were run. Test files count as coverage, not proof. No score of 5 was given.

The packet filter dropped files. The BORG .mjs/.js files (conductor, router, Inbox web UI, planner) and adapter metadata were fetched read-only from public commit 57ae994 and hash-verified (61 of 61) against the in-packet RELEASE-INVENTORY.json. 22 dropped Omnara files were fetched from public commit 9f9ef08, and one reviewer read two more (gateway.nginx.conf, .env.example with values masked) from the same commit's git objects.

Not inspected: Omnara Cloud's private services (credential service, billing, the kill-switch writer); BORG adapter weights, site JS and the fleet_browser worker; Plimsoll dotfiles and CI, dashboard.html and the Cloud Prisma schema; the installed mem0ctl, recall-fast, Claude hook and graph binaries (the public copies stood in for them).

Runtime state is UNKNOWN: which memory flags are set (graph, JEV, capture student), which capture hook each harness runs, whether the backup schedule is installed, live Plimsoll linkage coverage today, and the Cloud signing configuration.

Ecosystem capabilities (shared hub, fleet conductors, Estate Ops, account recovery, secrets hub) are documented in the fleet tools directory but not verified. The lead checks BORG runtime and fleet health separately. The only live evidence is from this session: the seat-gate admission probes, the Inbox and Jev hook contexts, and the delegated run itself.
Plimsoll and Plimsoll Cloud are working-tree snapshots that may include uncommitted changes, so no public commit links are given for them.

Five read-only Opus reviewer subagents gathered the evidence. I re-read about 35 high-impact citations and found no errors, but did not exhaustively re-verify every reviewer citation. Claims marked 'reviewer' in AUDIT.md rest on reviewer reads.
Inferred, not reproduced: Omnara's head-of-line wakeup hazard, the effect of macOS os.freemem on BORG admission, and when the router ledger fills. The entry and byte limits are verified.
Mem0 recall was deliberately not used, to keep this audit independent of other audits and lead opinions, so prior decisions recorded only in memory may be unaccounted for.

Scores are expert judgment for James's use case, not benchmarks. Criticality weights reflect my reading of his operating policy (reliability, admission, allowance routing, receipts) and are open to the lead's calibration.
